segments.text: Start here. What you are about to see.
This is a research project. It is building a language model: a program that reads text and writes an answer.
Two of its goals: skills and careful thinking first, then learning from only a few examples.
It is not an app. GitHub lists 0 releases for it, and nothing here is finished.
First goal: skills and careful thinking.
At the smallest size, 3 million learned numbers, an earlier design scored higher than an ordinary same-size model in all six separate training runs.
Second goal: learning from only a few examples. Only partly shown so far: brand-new kinds of rule are mostly missed.
The reader gives each letter a meaning from the whole question. Its main part is borrowed from others and frozen: our practice never changes it.
The thinker thinks in rounds, which are laps of looking and thinking. Our practice sets its settings from scratch.
The stop switch says done. It is built, but never run.
The talker writes one line a turn. Today it is a small stand-in.
Outside: a calculator. The talker's line calls it; the reader reads the reply.
One picture runs through the whole video: a student doing a word problem.
A translator reads the question. A team of note-takers thinks it over, round after round.
The one who writes the final answer may write a request slip. A pocket calculator, outside the team, hands back a slip, and the translator reads it.
A little bell rings when they are done. One person writes the final answer. Each colour always means the same part.
Green: tested. A result file exists. Example: with the calculator outside, scores matched the earlier design in six runs, at the smallest size.
Amber: built, but never tested. The code exists, but no real training run was ever done. Example: the stop switch.
Grey: placeholder. It does not exist yet. Example: the English talker.
A vector is a list of numbers, like a note card. The reader turns each letter into one. “Picture only” means a drawing, not a measurement.
A round is one lap of looking at the whole question, passing notes, and thinking. The thinker does several laps.
A call is the talker's line: a text request to the outside calculator. Here, sub 12 5 means: take 5 away from 12.
The reply is the calculator's answer, also text: 7. The whole reader reads it. Together they read sub 12 5 = 7.
The talker writes calls on its own. A line that is not a call is the final answer.
Practice: the model tries a question, is told the right answer, and every setting is nudged a tiny bit. One nudge is one update.
Questions kept aside are never used in practice. They are saved for the exam, so the score is fair: the model has never seen them.
A score is points out of 100: the share of questions answered right. Here, 73.01 points on 6,040 questions kept aside.
A copy is one separate run of the model from its own random start. Six copies are six chances to see the same result.
Careful: 73.01 is one copy, at the smallest size, on an earlier design.
A plain model is an ordinary model of the same size, trained on the same practice, with the same borrowed reader. It is our yardstick.
On the same 6,040 questions kept aside, the plain model scored 67.12 points out of 100, and ours scored 73.01.
Careful: these two scores come from one copy, at the smallest size, on an earlier design. We do not claim it holds at bigger sizes.
Every real number in this video comes from a project file. Here is one example: the plain model's score, traced to its file.
Pictures that only illustrate carry a tag, like picture only or made-up example. They are never real measurements.
What is not proven stays amber or grey. Nothing here is released, and no future date is promised to you.
Part 1 of 10. One question, start to finish.
This chapter follows one question through the whole model.
The model has four parts: reader, thinker, stop switch and talker. It uses an outside calculator.
Some parts have a test result. All together, never tested.
Here is the question. We made it up as an example.
The model works on letters, so every letter gets its own box.
The question has 71 characters, spaces included.
A borrowed reader (trained by someone else) reads the whole question once. Its name is EmbeddingGemma 2.
Frozen means our practice (training) never changes it.
Each letter gets 768 numbers from the reader: those of the word piece the letter sits in.
The reader has 271,002,624 numbers. We did not set them.
A small learned window lets each letter see 4 letters on each side.
It is ours, learned from scratch in our practice.
In small tests at the 3 million size, every reader without it failed the letter-code puzzles.
The thinker is the part that loops. One lap around the question is one round.
In each round it looks at the whole question, passes notes, and thinks.
The same learned settings are used every round. Only its notes change.
In round 1 the thinker looks at every letter and passes notes.
Tested version: no call (a request to the calculator) is written after round 1; the call slot stays empty.
In the version we tested, the first call comes after round 2.
Tested version: after round 2 the call writer reads its first control vector (a list of numbers).
It picks one of 8 operations, or writes no call. No call is a choice.
The 8 are add, sub, mul, div, mod, min, max and cmp.
Tested version: the thinker writes a call as text. A learned pointer finds each number's last digit.
The code copies one letter at a time to the left, until the learned stop head says stop.
Some steps are still hand-written code, like flipping the digits into reading order.
The calculator is an ordinary program. It is outside the model.
A call is a line of text. The reader reads the answer, also as text.
With the calculator switched off, questions that need a calculation scored 0.0 points out of 100 on all 6 copies.
The outside calculator gets sub 12 5 and sends back 7, as plain text.
Built so far: the letter window alone reads the reply. New design: the whole reader, Gemma too.
Gemma and the calculator have never run together.
Round 3 now also sees sub 12 5 = 7.
Tested version: the call writer writes add 7 3, copying 7 from the reply and 3 from the question.
The calculator returns 10. The reader reads it, and it joins the notes.
Some rounds have nothing to calculate, so they write no call.
In the version we tested, calls come after rounds 2 to 8 only.
The newest version can call in any round from 2 to 32. Built, not tested.
After each round a small learned switch asks: is it done yet?
It must run at least 1 round, and at most 32. The 32 is a safety limit.
A stop ends each turn. The switch is built, never tested.
The stand-in copies 10 from the last reply, where the thinker points.
It adds no thinking of its own, so the answer is just the copied 10.
The planned talker, about 25 million numbers, reads thoughts, no pointer, and writes calls.
Green: adding the Gemma reader gained 2.67 points out of 100 (6,040 questions) in 6 of 6 copies at 3M.
Green: calculator outside matched the old calculator-inside model in 6 copies. One check on no-thinking answers missed; the project owner cleared it.
Amber: calls in any round, stop switch. Built, never tested.
Grey: the English talker. A placeholder, not built yet.
Open question: with the Gemma reader, some answers use zero thinking rounds. Everything together: never tested.
The reader reads each turn's new text. The thinker thinks in rounds.
The stop switch ends the turn. The talker writes the answer or a call.
Now we open each box, one at a time.
Part 2 of 10. The reader: giving every letter a meaning.
The question enters the reader first. The reader is a borrowed model called Gemma, and it reads the whole question one time.
Picture only: a translator who already knows English well. We borrowed him, and we cannot change him.
Gemma cuts text into word pieces, called tokens.
Our thinker, the part that does the thinking, works on letters: one spot for each letter.
On 20,000 of our skill questions, one token covers 3.08 letters on average.
On 9,068 web-text chunks of 279 letters, one token covers 4.27 letters on average.
Gemma reads the whole question one time.
Each token gets a row of 768 numbers that holds its meaning in context.
Each letter takes the row of the token it sits in.
The reader holds 271,002,624 numbers, all set before our work began.
134,217,728 of them are a word table (one row per word piece); 136,784,896 are reading layers (a transformer) plus a step widening rows to 768.
It is frozen: our practice never changes it. Its own reading limit is 8,192 tokens, which is not our limit.
In the small test models, a converter plug, one learned layer, turns Gemma's 768 numbers into the thinker's width.
At width 256 it has 196,864 learned numbers. At full size there is no plug: Gemma's 512 numbers go straight in.
First: which letter it is. A learned row of numbers.
Second: where it sits in the question. A learned table: 2,000 rows in the planned finished design (B3), 280 in the growth test (G1).
Third: how far its letter sits from the end of its word. The count is hand-written; the row it picks is learned.
Fourth: Gemma's meaning is added on top, via a small plug (none at full size). The letter window reads the sum.
Two small learned layers read the summed row. They are ours, not borrowed.
Each layer looks 2 letters left and 2 right, so together a letter sees 4 letters each side.
The window adds about 0.7 million numbers at width 256, about 2.6 million at 512.
Letter-cipher puzzles are one kind of test question: 40 familiar-style ones per copy (a separate training run), scored out of 100.
With the window, Gemma plus letters scores 97.5 and 95.0 on two copies.
Without it, Gemma plus letters scores 5.0 and 2.5.
Letters alone, without it, score 12.5 and 2.5.
The position table has one row per spot, so it sets the longest question: 280 letters in the growth test (G1), 2,000 in planned B3.
In a sample of 4,000 bAbI test questions (a public set of story puzzles), 32% run over 280 letters and 1% over 2,000.
Tested version: a hand-written pattern finds numbers. The new design copies none.
It records where each number is, not its value.
Room to mark: 16 numbers in the calculator-outside model (T1SDR), 91 in the growth test (G1), 240 in planned B3.
New design: each calculator reply, shown as sub 12 5 = 7, is read by Gemma plus the letter window.
Built B3 version: the window alone reads replies.
Never tested. The old reason, that Gemma adds nothing to a reply, was only suggested.
On 6,040 test questions kept aside (five kinds, called Pooled-5), six separate training runs (copies) with the reader scored 75.9 to 77.2.
Eight copies of the same model without the reader scored 73.0 to 74.7.
On average the reader is ahead by 2.67 points out of 100, in all 6 copies (seeds), at 3M (about 3 million learned numbers).
A leak means some answers are right with zero rounds of thinking.
Averaged over 6 copies, the zero-round leak is 6.59. The pass mark, set in advance as the no-reader average plus 1.0, was 4.62. Missed.
On seed 200, on familiar questions, the reader version scored 18.09 with zero rounds; the same model without it, 1.40.
Copies without the reader leak on some seeds too, so the cause is not settled.
A test called TK would let the thinker read one spot per token (word piece) instead of one per letter.
The code and a PC job file exist, but it has never been run, so there is no result. Letters or tokens is still undecided.
The reader is borrowed and frozen. It reads the question once.
Each letter gets a meaning in context, plus a window of 4 letters each side.
Without the window, the Gemma version scored 5.0 and 2.5 out of 100 on cipher puzzles, in two copies.
Part 3 of 10. The thinker: rounds of looking and passing notes.
This is the thinker, the second part of the model. It does the thinking.
It is ours. It starts from scratch and learns only from our practice.
The planned size is about 100 million numbers. That size has never been tested.
Picture only. Think of a small team of note-takers sitting around one question.
Each round, every note-taker looks at the whole question again.
Then they pass notes to each other and write down what they now believe.
The same team, with the same habits, every round.
A vector is a list of numbers, like a note card with a row of numbers.
The thinker keeps 8 control vectors. Two of them steer the work.
It also keeps 36 memory vectors, where its notes are kept.
Older builds had 17 vectors: 8 control and 9 memory.
In the tested version, after each round from round 2 on, the call writer reads control vector 0.
It either writes a request for the outside calculator, like sub 12 5, or writes nothing.
The numbers in the request are usually copied from the question or an earlier reply.
Controls 2 to 7 feed no output. They only pass information along when the notes look at each other.
In an older build, switching them off at test time cost 1.6 points on the main test.
On the multi-step test they cost 7.8 points: 99.4 fell to 91.6.
Those numbers are one copy (seed 200). All six copies of that older design lost points, very unevenly.
Each letter of the question is one box. A borrowed reader, Gemma, has already given each letter its meaning.
Each note vector looks at every letter. Later it also looks at each reply the whole reader has read.
The shading inside each note is a picture only, not real numbers.
Step 2: the note vectors look at each other. In code this is called self-attention.
Each note reads the other notes and keeps what matters from them.
The letters are not compared with each other inside the thinker.
Step 3: each note goes through a small network.
At the 100M step it widens to 4.8 times as many numbers, then squeezes back.
Then the notes go on to the next round.
One look, compare and think unit is a block. The same blocks run in every round.
The learned numbers are the same in every round. Same team, same habits.
A round stamp, a learned tag for the round number, is added to the notes each round.
Tested version. Tom has 12 apples, gives away 5, then buys 3. After round 2, the call writer writes sub 12 5.
It copies 12 and 5. The outside calculator replies 7. The reader reads it, and adds it to the notes.
Round 3 sees that reply. After it, the call writer writes add 7 3, and the calculator replies 10.
Today's stand-in talker copies 10; the planned one has no pointer. New design: the talker writes calls, and replies start the next turn.
After each round, a tiny learned stop switch, the bell, asks: is this settled, or should it think more?
It must think at least 1 round. It can never go past 32 rounds.
It learns from a settled label: stop once no later round would have been right.
A block is one look, compare and think unit, built from attention and a small network.
Counting every learned number in one block, where each vector holds 512 numbers (its width), gives 4,624,281.
Our arithmetic: 21 blocks alone give 97.1 million. An older plan said 30 blocks, which would give about 139 million.
The learned part of the model comes in four sizes, named 3M, 10M, 30M and 100M for their rough size.
These are counts from the build. The finished design (B3) has not been run at any of these sizes yet.
As built so far, without the planned talker, the whole model at the 100 million step is 373.1 million numbers, borrowed reader included.
An average question has 81 letters. Every letter against every letter: 81 times 81 is 6,561 checks.
Notes look at letters instead. A rough count: 44 notes, each looking at 81 letters and 27 number slots, gives 4,752 checks per round.
Over 8 rounds, the older count, that is 4,752 times 8 = 38,016. At 81 letters, no work is saved.
Its gain is structure, not speed. By this count, much longer text would favour the notes, but that is untested.
In the first completed test (older design), one copy at the smallest size scored 73.01 points out of 100 on 6,040 kept-aside questions, thinking on.
With thinking switched off (zero rounds), the same copy scored 0.66 points.
That is one copy at one size. Part 8 explains the test and its checks.
Not known: the thinker has never been tested at 100 million numbers.
Not known: whether many rounds hurt. One older probe, on one seed, found 16 rounds cost 1.2 to 1.9 points.
Experts (many small specialist networks, a few used at a time) are a separate idea, not yet tested and not covered here.
Remember: the thinker looks, passes notes and thinks, in rounds. The same blocks run every round. A learned bell is built to say when to stop.
Part 4 of 10. Asking the calculator for help.
In the new design, the talker's line calls the calculator, an outside tool, at the end of a turn. The reply starts the next turn, and the whole reader reads it.
Rule (project rules, Oct 7): hand-written code may run only as an outside tool that the model chooses to call.
Code adds two numbers exactly, every time.
A learned network has to learn each sum from practice.
In the new design, the talker writes its sum on a text slip (made-up numbers here) and sends it to a calculator outside the model. The whole reader reads the reply.
In the tested version, after a round (one lap of the thinker), the call writer reads the thinker's first control vector, a list of numbers.
It writes one of nine choices: no call, or one of the eight operations. The new design drops this call writer: the talker writes the call.
The outside calculator has eight operations, with made-up numbers 12 and 5. We worked out each result by hand; ? means the call cannot run.
In the tested version, to write the 12 in a call, the call writer's learned pointer lands on its last digit, the 2.
The copy then steps one letter left and copies the 1.
A learned stop head says when to stop.

In the tested version, the copy trick was used for 98% of written operands and, by today's stand-in talker, for 91.5% of answers, on all six separate copies (T1SDR). The planned talker and the new design use no pointer or copying.
Copied here means the copy trick was used, not that the copy was right.
In the tested version, some call numbers are in neither the question nor a reply, and the call writer builds such a number one digit at a time.
Tested copies had 11 cells. The never-run build of the finished design has 21, last digit first; the code flips the text. The new design has no call writer.
The calculator is ordinary Python code, outside the model. It has 0 learned numbers.
In the new design, it reads a call (made-up numbers here) and writes the reply as text, which starts the next turn for the whole reader. A call it cannot run gets a question mark.
In the tested version, in our made-up Tom example, after round 2 the call writer writes sub 12 5 as text, and the outside calculator replies.
The reply, sub 12 5 = 7, comes back as text. In the tested version the reader's letter window reads it, and it is added to the notes. The new design uses the whole reader, Gemma plus the window.
The question is not read again. After round 3 the call writer writes add 7 3, and the calculator replies 10.
In the tested version, the first call follows round 2.
Call k follows round k plus 1, up to call 7 after round 8.
The tested copies ran 8 rounds. In the built learned-stop code, rounds 9 to 32 cannot call.
The project owner chose any time for when a call may follow.
The finished design's first build lets a call follow any round from 2 to 32.
The tape (the list of calls and replies so far) holds 16 calls.
In training, 1 row in 4 gets 0, 1 or 2 extra thinking rounds before each call.
In the call-writer builds, some parts are still ordinary code a person wrote. Four of them are shown here in brown boxes.
The operation name comes from a fixed list of 8, so a new tool could not be called yet.
The finished design's second build writes the whole call as letters, operation name included.
It is built as code and has never run.
Each copy starts from its own random start.
The tested version, T1SDR, where the calculator is an outside tool, was compared with a similar model, B2, where the calculator is inside.
Pooled-5 (6,040 questions kept aside), T1SDR minus B2: plus 0.62; likely range minus 0.23 to plus 1.46.
No copy fell over 1.0 below B2. The range includes 0: no clear difference.
Chain-5, 1,000 multi-step questions: 99.6 to 99.8 with the calculator outside, mean 99.72. Inside: 99.4 to 99.7.
Calculator switched off: the 2,085 questions that need it score 0.0.
Swap test: add and sub are secretly swapped inside the calculator. The answer should follow the new reply.
Pass line: 99% or more of counted rows follow the swap. Rows with two possible sources are not counted.
Five copies: 99.28 to 99.87, all at 99 or more.
The run's own first reading was 97.1 to 97.6. Its scoring rule was corrected after the misses were studied.
The sixth copy's saved model was lost, so it is not scored.
Leak check: swap in another question's thinking, then count answers still right, out of 100 (1,360 questions).
Limit written down before the run: 5. Five of six copies read above it, from 5.07 to 5.59.
B2 (calculator inside) read 3.09 to 3.75 on the same check.
It failed the limit. The project owner cleared it on Oct 9; it is disclosed, not a clean pass.
Separate reading, zero rounds of thinking: one copy read 12.94, against 10.81 for B2.
Tested version: the calculator outside the model, at 3M, over six copies (swap check on five; leak check cleared by the owner).
Never run together: the borrowed Gemma reader with the outside calculator.
Built, never run: calls at any round.
Remember: in the new design (being built), the talker's line calls the calculator and the whole reader reads the reply. The tested version used a copy trick, with a learned stop.
Part 5 of 10. Deciding when it is done.
The model thinks in rounds, one lap at a time.
The stop switch decides when thinking stops.
It is built, but it has never been run.
The older design had a dial: the same number of rounds for every question, set by hand (12 in the tested model, 8 in another).
Easy questions may need fewer rounds. Hard questions may need more.
We turned the dial down on one trained copy, with no new practice.
Points out of 100, on 6,040 questions kept aside (called pooled-5).
Trained at 12 rounds it scored 73.01. With 2 rounds, 29.30. With 1 round, 20.00. With 0 rounds, 0.66.
Chain-5 is a set of 1,000 multi-step questions, scored on the same trained copy.
On pooled-5, 1 round scored 20.00. On chain-5 it scored 0.0, and 1.1 at 2 rounds.
At the full 12 rounds chain-5 scored 99.9. So this copy needed more rounds on multi-step questions than on pooled-5.
Older models were trained for 8 rounds. In a round-count test on two copies, the score on practice-like questions stopped rising at 8 rounds.
On all 8 copies we checked (those two and six more), running 16 rounds scored 0.8 to 1.9 points lower than 8 rounds.
So too few rounds hurt, and too many may hurt too.
After every round, the stop switch, a small head, reads one of the thinker's note cards.
It gives a number from 0 to 1. At 0.5 or more, the thinking stops.
It always runs at least 1 round, and never more than 32.
The stop switch has 257 numbers when each card has 256, and 513 when each has 512.
Built version: one stop for the whole answer. New design: one stop per turn.
Built version, not tested: the thinker may call an outside calculator, from round 2 up to 32.
Built code: about a quarter of questions add 0 to 2 rounds before a call. New design: the talker writes calls.
Training gives every round a label: stop, or keep going.
The label says stop when the answer is right now, or when no later round is right.
So the stop switch is also taught to stop on questions it cannot solve.
Practice uses batches of questions, and some batches run only 8 rounds. There, a question first right at round 10 looks never right.
So the label says stop at round 1, and the stop switch would learn to stop too early.
Fix: the stop switch learns only from batches that run all 32 rounds, about 1 in 4.
The label only sees the rounds a question actually ran.
So a stop that fires early may never be shown a later right answer (suggested).
The first run is planned to report how often questions stop early, and their answers. This is reported only, not a pass mark.
Key pass marks (bars the test must reach) were written before any run. They are targets, not results.
On average, 1-step questions must use at most half the rounds of the longest ones (code: 11 steps; plan: 12).
Always-32 is the same model forced to think all 32 rounds. Practised questions: within 1 point. Longer chains: within 2.
It fails if it never stops early (rounds within 10% of 32), or if longer chains fall over 5 below always-32.
No build switch removes the stop. The switches cover things like Gemma and calls, not the stop.
A trained copy can still be run with the stop ignored and a forced number of rounds, as a test.
The nearest model with no stop is the outside-calculator model (T1SDR), with a fixed 8 rounds.
The stop has never run. Its first run is planned after the separate G1 size test finishes (not covered here).
People talk about fast thinking and slow thinking. Few rounds is like the fast kind, many rounds like the slow kind.
We suggest one looped thinker gives both, so no separate fast and slow model is needed (suggested, not tested).
To remember: the stop switch decides, the limit is 32 rounds, and the stop is built but not yet run.
Part 6 of 10. Writing down the answer.
This is the last part inside the model: the talker.
Its only job is to write each turn's last line. It adds no thinking.
New design, untested: thoughts in, calls and answer out. No pointer.
Today's talker is a small stand-in. It also copies from the question and the notes, where the thinker points.
Today's talker is a small stand-in with three ways to write an answer.
Span copy takes a stretch of letters from the question or the notes.
A word pointer, a learned pick of a spot, takes one whole word from the question.
Letter slots spell the answer when it is not in the text. The planned talker has no pointer.
In today's stand-in, a pointer lands on the last digit of the last reply: the 0.
The copy steps one letter left and takes the 1.
Next to the left is a space. A small learned part, the stop head, says stop.
The digits came out last first, 0 then 1. Plain code flips them to read 10. The plan has no pointer.
In the tested version, in all 6 copies of the 3-million-number model with an outside calculator (T1SDR), the stand-in's span copy wrote 91.5% of answers.
That counts how often it was used on 400 familiar calculator questions, not how often it was right.
The stand-in's pointer and stop head are learned. Three small pieces are hand-written code.
The plan: one learned writer, for calls and answers, replaces them. Not run.
When the answer is not in the text, today's stand-in spells it in letter slots.
Today there are 9 places: room for 8 letters and an end mark. Each place picks a letter, or copies one.
They fill last letter first, so yes comes out as s, e, y. The code flips it.
Today's letter slots hold 8 letters. A longer training answer would be cut to 8.
That never happened: 0 of 200,000 training answers were longer than 8.
But hiding a word of 9 to 12 letters, in fill-in-the-blank practice, would hit it.
The finished design (B3) writes up to 35 letters and counts any longer answer.
A count above 0 fails its pass mark, set in advance. Blanks of 9 to 12 letters are safe only here.
The plan's talker, about 25 million numbers (25M), reads the thinker's final thoughts and writes English, with no pointer.
It is not built. As built, the 100M-thinker design is 373.1M in all: 271.0M borrowed, frozen reader (Gemma) plus 102.1M trained.
How it would learn to write English is not in the plan. A separate team session owns that.
These tests are older, from a design built on borrowed language models. Not today's talker.
With a 350-million-number language model as reader and talker, our system scored 66.1. With 1.2 billion: 92.6.
A small copy talker scored 13.6 on question kinds it never practised. The language-model talker scored 78.2.
One check turned the thinking off on one trained copy at 3M. This is the older design: calculator inside, 12 rounds.
Thinking on scored 73.01. Thinking off scored 0.66, on 6,040 questions kept aside.
That hints the talker cannot answer alone. One copy is only a hint.
An earlier Gemma-reader copy scored 18.09 on familiar questions with zero rounds, so 'cannot' is not shown.
Free web text, called FineWeb-Edu, enters practice as fill-in-the-blank rows.
One word of 3 to 12 letters is hidden, and the model must name it.
So this kind of practice teaches reading English, not writing it.
By plan, 84% of the practice text in the planned big training run is web text.
The plan's final proof is a race against small public models, such as SmolLM2-360M.
To win, it must be ahead by at least 3 points on our own kept-aside tests, and ahead on a question set called bAbI.
The whole size is counted, borrowed numbers too. The race needs the English talker, which does not exist yet.
The plan: thoughts in, calls and answer out, no pointer.
Today's stand-in copies by pointer. Tested only at 3M.
The English talker is a placeholder. Today's model gives short answers, not sentences.
Part 7 of 10. Practice, one small nudge at a time.
Practice sets the numbers inside the thinker, the stop switch (built, not yet run) and the talker (a small stand-in so far; in the new design it writes the calls).
The borrowed reader stays frozen. The outside calculator is plain code and needs no practice.
The model tries a question.
It is shown the right answer.
Then every learned setting moves a tiny bit. One nudge is one update.
Each update looks at 256 practice rows, then nudges every learned setting once.
The 3M test copy, with 3.5 million learned settings, did 24,000 updates.
Our multiplication: 24,000 × 256 = 6,144,000 row draws. The pool has 1,418,702 rows, so rows come round again.
AdamW is the nudging rule. The learning rate is how big a nudge may be.
It starts small, peaks at 1e-3 after a 300-update warm-up, then falls to 10% of the peak.
Sums run in short numbers (bf16), rows come shuffled, and the start is random.
The 3M test copy practised on a pool of 60 million pieces of text (GPT-2 word pieces).
By word pieces: own text 38%, web text 62%. By rows: own 811,663, web 607,039.
Our rows: skills questions and English passages made by our code, plus teaching rows (TEACH) a 1.2-billion-number teacher model wrote earlier.
FineWeb-Edu web text: a script blanks one word of 3 to 12 letters, and the model must name it.
Each prompt holds at most 280 letters, blank included, in the 3M runs; the finished design's long pool goes up to 2,000.
It learns to read English, not write it. Rows without steps add a faint no-call label, weight 0.1.
Built version: where a row has worked steps, the key gives the right call each round.
Call loss: was the call slip right? After the last call, the right slip is no call.

Part 9 of 10. Learning while it sleeps.
People sort out the day's lessons while they sleep.
This model gets a night too: a day of practice, then a night of study.
Sleep is not a sixth part. It is a way of learning, tested so far only in research on earlier-design copies.
By day the model gets puzzles with a hidden rule: 2 gives 5, 4 gives 9, 7 gives 15.
It tries rules. A try counts only if it fits every example, so no answer key is needed.
Only x times 2 plus 1 fits all three, so 10 gives 21. That try is kept, and the night studies it.
The old sleep scored 71.3 out of 100 on first tries and needed 558 to 610 updates by its formula. An update is a small nudge to every setting.
The newer sleep used 256 updates a night and averaged 76.1 over six copies.
But this is not a paired comparison. 71.3 is the old sleep's stored number, from its own near-copy starting copies. Each copy slept once.
The model makes its own tries, then sleeps for 256 updates of 1,024 rows. A row is one practice question.
Half the rows are fresh dreams: new questions written from a program it found, so none is read twice. Half are fresh skills rows.
Every 32 updates it checks itself on 128 held questions, and keeps its best saved model.
Did old skills get worse than before the sleep? No. Pooled over the six copies they rose by 0.52 points, likely range 0.31 to 0.74.
But a control that only practised the same skills rows raised them by 2.11, range 1.88 to 2.32.
So sleep did not beat plain practice: sleep minus control is −1.58. The gain is not shown to come from the sleep.

Part 10 of 10. Creative mode: what it does when it gets stuck.
Picture yourself stuck on a puzzle. What do you do?
You try an idea, check it, and try another one.
Our model can do the same, but only when it is stuck.
First the model makes one careful best-guess try, with creative mode switched off.
Then it checks that try on the question's own examples.
If the try does not fit the examples, the model counts itself stuck.
Only then does it try lots of ideas: 32 sampled tries.
If none of the 32 fits, it gets 480 more, so 512 in all.
A question it already solved gets no extra tries.
A checker runs every try on the examples that came with the question. It needs no answer key.
A try that fits every example is kept. The rest are thrown away.
For each question it keeps at most 2 different fitting tries.
We tried it on an older small design, on two trial copies, with development questions.
The search worked: it found 180 and 237 checked tries on multi-step questions. The bars were 75 and 90.
After two nights, first-try scores on multi-step questions rose 10.4 and 9.7 points. The bar was 10.
Copy B gained 15 of 154 questions where 16 were needed. Not a pass, and not proved wrong.
At night it practises on its own checked tries. That is the sleep from Part 9.
